basis: R1 control test: American Pathology Partners was incorporated in February 2008 by three laboratory and hospital executives and in April 2008 secured a $75M equity commitment from NEA, the only investor named, then bought UniPath (Denver, December 2008), Eastern Carolina Pathology (2009) and Palm Beach Pathology's technical operation (2011) (Wikipedia). A single sponsor's equity commitment to a company formed to buy operating labs is a control position, not a minority financing. NEA's own percentage is not published, hence medium; flagged.

R1 control test: NEA's 2021 entry was leading a $300M investment in AllyAlign Health beside Oak HC/FT, Town Hall Ventures and existing investors Heritage Group and Ziegler, reported as a new investment that brought in Mark Price as CEO (Skilled Nursing News, 2021-06-10). In May 2022 AllyAlign, Elite Patient Care and Provider Health Services combined as Curana Health, which the firm's own post calls an NEA company formation. The record shows a syndicated financing, not a purchase of the company from its owners, and no record gives NEA a majority, so NEA holds a minority from a financing and the row is a member at Growth. Flagged: the firm's 'company formation' wording also covers Radiology Partners and Strive Health.

note: Senior-living primary care and Medicare Advantage company. NEA entered in June 2021 by leading a $300M investment in AllyAlign Health with Oak HC/FT, Town Hall Ventures, Heritage Group and Ziegler, which brought in Mark Price as CEO (Skilled Nursing News); in May 2022 AllyAlign, Elite Patient Care and Provider Health Services united as Curana Health (the firm's post of 2022-05-04). Growth on the firm's own card.

basis: R1 control test: Frazier Healthcare Partners bought Comprehensive Pharmacy Services from NexPhase Capital, closing in March 2019 (NexPhase's exit to a financial sponsor, March 2019; Middle Market Growth). The firm gives its own first investment as 2019 with Mohamad Makhzoumi on the board, and the Private Equity Stakeholder Project's June 2022 table names Frazier Healthcare Partners and New Enterprise Associates among the owners when Trellis Rx bought the company. NEA entered beside Frazier in the buyout (the Frazier and NEA pairing of DSI Renal, Elements and RevSpring), so its co-investor group acquired control. No record gives NEA's own share, hence medium.

R1 control test, carve-out purchase: TriVascular was sold to Boston Scientific in 2005, and in March 2008 TV2 Holding Company 'acquired BSSR from Boston Scientific Corporation', paying partly with a $3.5M note (2014 S-1). The TV2 Series A that funded the purchase was about half NEA 12's (32.4M of 64.9M Series A shares in the S-1 holder table), and NEA's Jake Nunn joined the board in March 2008. The investor group bought the business outright, a control purchase rather than a minority financing. Flagged: if a venture syndicate's carve-out of a pre-revenue device business is ruled a venture entry, the row is a member at Series A (March 2008). Same company as the member row tv2-holding-co, which should follow this verdict.

R1 control test, carve-out purchase: Xcel Pharmaceuticals was founded in January 2001 to buy Elan's Diastat (worldwide) and Mysoline (US) product lines, acquired in March and April 2001 for a net $149.7M, $99M of it lent by Elan and the rest from its own equity, the Series A of March 2001 (IPO registration, January 2002). Domain Partners V (5.1M shares) and NEA 10 (5.0M) together held about 54% of the 18.7M shares outstanding, so the Series A investors, NEA among them, controlled a company formed to buy an operating product business. Flagged: if a venture-syndicated purchase of a product line is read as a financing, the row is a member at Series A (2001-03-30), as its classification already reads.

R1 control test not decidable. The firm lists ECI Acquisition Holdings (ECi Software Solutions, Fort Worth business software for distributors and manufacturers, operating since the early 1980s) with a 2006 first investment and the label Early, and the page first appears in the Common Crawl of early 2014 (CC-MAIN-2014-10), around when Carlyle bought ECi (Carlyle release, 2014-03-12). ECI Acquisition Holdings, Inc. is that buyout's holding company: Golub Capital BDC's 10-Q for the quarter to March 2014 carries its one-stop loans maturing 03/2019 and a common stock position. What NEA bought in 2006 (a minority growth round, or a stake later rolled into Carlyle's holding company) is in no record read. If the position is a rollover into the buyout it is out under control_position; if a 2006 minority round, a member at Growth. Left for review.

R1 control test: Frazier Healthcare Partners bought RevSpring from GTCR in March 2024, and 'Frazier was joined in the deal by NEA, 22C Capital, and RevSpring's senior leadership team' (Pulse 2.0, 2024-03-13). NEA was part of the buyer group that acquired the company, a control transaction, not a minority financing.

R1 control test: Elements Behavioral Health (incorporated in 2007 as Subacute Holdings) sold $62.8M of an $80M offering from 2008-01-30 with NEA's Chip Linehan and Mohamad Makhzoumi and two Frazier Healthcare Ventures partners as directors (Form D), and in 2008 bought Promises Treatment Centers for about $30M, a purchase Frazier Healthcare Ventures and New Enterprise Associates 'helped cover' (Los Angeles Business Journal, 2010). A company the two sponsors funded to buy an operating business, the DSI Renal pattern, so out as a control position. Same company as the member row ebh-holding-company-inc, which should follow this verdict.

R1 control test: on 2018-06-01 NEA funds acquired, through NEAPH Holdings (later Everside Health Holdings), all of the outstanding equity interests of DaVita's direct primary care business, Paladina, for about $60.0M in cash (Everside Health's 2021 draft S-1, Certain Relationships). A buyout of the whole company, not a round. Same position as everside-health (already not_member) and marathon-health.

R1 control test: the firm's Marathon Health page (2018, Growth) is the Paladina position. Paladina, renamed Everside Health, merged with Marathon Health on 2024-02-08 under the Marathon name, with existing shareholders including General Atlantic, New Enterprise Associates and Oak HC/FT backing the combined company (PR Newswire). NEA never financed Marathon itself, which General Atlantic bought in 2019; its Marathon stock came from combining a company it bought outright from DaVita in 2018, so the row is out as that control position.

Not D8. Mayfield, New Enterprise Associates and Melchor Venture put $1.1M into 3Com on 1981-02-27, its first venture financing (History of Computer Communications), and the firm's own 2012 post names 'the funding of Bob Metcalfe and 3Com' as its nominee for NEA's most consequential tech investment. The firm's year 1996 is when 3Com bought OnStream Networks (the onstream row, NEA 1991), whose 3Com stock was sale consideration, but NEA had funded 3Com itself fifteen years earlier, so the row is a member on the 1981 round.

note: Networking company acquired by Hewlett-Packard in 2010, Marlborough by then (as the Sequoia row reads). NEA, Mayfield and Melchor Venture put $1.1M into 3Com on 1981-02-27, its first venture financing, and the firm's 2012 post calls the funding of Bob Metcalfe and 3Com its most consequential tech investment. The firm's year 1996 is 3Com's purchase of OnStream Networks (the onstream row). The 1981 round is not named in the record, so the stage stays undetermined.

basis: D8: NEA's Cornelius Bond sat on the board of Advanced Interventional Systems (LAIS) from 1986 until June 1994, when LAIS merged into Spectranetics, and joined Spectranetics' board at that merger (2001 proxy). No record shows an NEA fund in Spectranetics before the merger, and the firm's 2013 historical page gives no year, so the holding is stock received for LAIS. Advanced Interventional Systems is the member; it is not in base.json (a recall gap).

D8: NEA 10 received 1,880,824 Pharmos shares on 2006-10-25 in exchange for its Series D preferred and notes of Vela Pharmaceuticals under the merger agreement of March 2006 (NEA's 13D, 2006-11-06); Pharmos was already listed on Nasdaq. Vela Pharmaceuticals is the member; it is not in base.json (a recall gap). NEA's later own money went into Pharmos' 10% convertible debentures (January 2008) and a common stock private placement (April 2009), both into a listed company, so they are X1 listed purchases rather than a separate venture entry. Flagged with X1: if PIPEs are ruled venture entries, Pharmos enters at Growth in January 2008.

D8: WebSideStory, already listed, bought Avivo Corporation under a merger agreement of 2005-02-08 in which NEA's Charles Linehan was the Avivo holders' representative; NEA 10's 13G (event 2005-05-04) reports 1,340,766 WebSideStory shares, 7.15%, counted with the 3,123,149 shares issued under that merger. The stake is sale consideration for Avivo. Avivo Corporation is the member; it is not in base.json (a recall gap). The 2006 purchase of Visual Sciences, LLC gave NEA nothing (visual-sciences is already not_member).

D8, a share swap at a combination: NEA invested in Wallapop in 2015 (the wallapop row), and in May 2016 Letgo merged with Wallapop's US operations, the merged company majority-owned by Letgo, with $100M of new money from Letgo's existing investors (Global Venturing, 2016-05-13), which names no NEA money. The firm's own posts call the holding 'Letgo (Wallapop)', its listing gives 2016 as the year, and Letgo's 2017 backer list carries Wallapop's investors (Accel, Eight Roads, Insight, Mangrove, NEA, Northzone; FashionNetwork, 2017-10-04). NEA's Letgo interest is consideration for Wallapop's US business, not a round it bought (the Point Nine madvertise precedent); no record read shows NEA money in a Letgo round. Wallapop is the member and is in base.json (row wallapop).

Not D8: no sale took place. GrubWithUs, Inc. (EDGAR CIK 1552345) is the corporation that became GOAT: it filed a Series A-7 preferred Form D from Culver City in 2016 under the GrubWithUs name and was renamed 1661, Inc., GOAT's operating company, before its February 2018 Series C filing ($58.75M, Index's Danny Rimer on the board). NEA's 2011 seed stock is stock of the company that pivoted, so the listing, which now links goat.com, is a member.

note: GrubWithUs, Inc. is the corporation that became GOAT (EDGAR: renamed 1661, Inc., GOAT's operating company, Culver City), so NEA's 2011 seed stock carries into GOAT; the dining product was shut, not the company. GOAT Group raised a $195M Series F led by Park West at a $3.7B valuation in June 2021 (Retail Dive), the last priced mark, stale. Stage from the firm's own label Seed. The a16z and First Round rows still read defunct. Graduation left for the graduation pass.

basis: R3 (D5): the firm's own page describes 'a medical device incubator'; the issuer is ExploraMed IV, L.L.C., a Mountain View LLC run by Josh Makower that sold $6.6M in 2011 (Form D). No source shows it operating as a company of its own; the device companies ExploraMed forms are judged on their own rows.

R3 (D5): the firm's own page describes a 'premier medical device incubator'; the issuer is ExploraMed V, L.L.C., which sold $8.8M in 2017 (Form D). No source shows it operating as a company of its own; the numbered NewCos ExploraMed forms (Willow, Revelle Aesthetics) are judged on their own rows.

R3 (D5): the firm's own page describes 'a medical device incubator focused on innovating and incubating novel medical technologies'; Prospex Medical III, Inc. (White Bear Lake, Minnesota; 2011 Form D, $1.5M sold, no revenue) is one of Robert Atkinson's numbered Prospex vehicles, a name that also appears on the Form D filings of BridgePoint Medical, Apnex Medical and ClarVista Medical. No source shows it operating as a company of its own.

R3 exception: the entity is itself an operating company. Foundry Therapeutics 1, Inc. (Menlo Park, CEO Karun Naga, $15.75M sold from 2019-01-31) was renamed Allay Therapeutics, Inc., the post-surgical pain company, under the same EDGAR CIK 1766366 (its 2021 Form D names Foundry Therapeutics 1 as the previous name). Same company as the listed member allay-therapeutics; identity-merges.json should fold this row into it.

note: Foundry Therapeutics 1, Inc. is Allay Therapeutics, Inc. renamed (same EDGAR CIK 1766366; the 2021 Form D names the previous name), the post-surgical pain company NEA also lists as allay-therapeutics; this row should merge into that one.
